title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 107 (Voting by show of hands)

content.overview: Section 107(1) provides that at any general meeting a resolution put to the vote shall, unless a poll is demanded under section 109 or the voting is carried out electronically, be decided on a show of hands. Section 107(2) makes a declaration by the Chairman of the passing or otherwise of the resolution by show of hands, and an entry to that effect in the minute books, conclusive evidence of the fact of passing of such resolution or otherwise.
content.glance: At a general meeting a resolution is decided on a show of hands in the first instance, unless a poll is demanded under section 109 or voting is carried out electronically. The chairman's declaration and the minute entry are conclusive evidence of the result on a show of hands.
content.study:
## Section 107 — voting by show of hands

**Subsection (1): default method.** At any general meeting, a resolution put to the vote of the meeting shall, unless a poll is demanded under section 109 or the voting is carried out electronically, be decided on a show of hands.

**Subsection (2): conclusive evidence.** A declaration by the Chairman of the meeting of the passing of a resolution or otherwise by show of hands under subsection (1), and an entry to that effect in the books containing the minutes of the meeting of the company, shall be conclusive evidence of the fact of passing of such resolution or otherwise.

## Apply the provision
- Confirm that the question is the voting method on a resolution at a general meeting.
- Check whether a poll has been demanded under section 109, or whether electronic voting applies under section 108 and the applicable rules; if either applies, the show-of-hands default does not decide the resolution.
- Where the show of hands is the method used, the chairman's declaration and the minute-book entry conclude the fact of the result; the statute does not require proof of the number or proportion of votes on a show of hands.
- Read section 107 with sections 106 (voting-right restrictions), 108 (electronic means) and 109 (demand for poll). Private-company application may be modified by the company's articles under the section 462 framework (G.S.R. 464(E) as amended), subject to the filing-default condition; that modification is a separate current-law check.

This note is a focused study aid; the topic remains under source and current-law review.

provisions.title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 107 (Voting by show of hands)

examples.title: Show of hands decides the resolution
examples.body: No poll is demanded under section 109 and electronic voting does not apply. The chairman declares the resolution carried and the minute book records that declaration. Section 107(2) treats the declaration and entry as conclusive evidence of the fact of passing. This is an educational illustration, not advice about a real dispute.

examples.title: Poll demand displaces the show of hands
examples.body: Before the result on a show of hands is treated as final, a valid demand for a poll is made under section 109. The show of hands does not conclude the resolution; the poll result is the decision. This is an educational illustration.

hypotheticals.question: At a general meeting the chairman declares a resolution carried on a show of hands and the minutes record that declaration. A member later asserts that a majority of votes by value were against the resolution. No poll was demanded and electronic voting did not apply. How should section 107 be analysed?
hypotheticals.analysis: Under subsection (1) the default method is a show of hands when no poll is demanded under section 109 and electronic voting does not apply. Subsection (2) makes the chairman's declaration and the minute entry conclusive evidence of the fact of passing. On the stated facts the statute does not require proof of the number or proportion of votes on the show of hands. Confirm that no valid poll demand was made and that electronic voting was not the method in use before relying on the conclusive-evidence rule.

hypotheticals.question: A poll is validly demanded under section 109 after a show of hands but before the result is treated as final. Does the show-of-hands declaration remain conclusive?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Subsection (1) itself excepts the case where a poll is demanded under section 109. Once a valid poll is ordered, the show of hands does not decide the resolution; the poll result does. Section 107(2) addresses the conclusive effect of a declaration on a show of hands, not a poll.

misconceptions.trap: Treating the chairman's show-of-hands declaration as conclusive even after a valid poll demand under section 109.
misconceptions.correction: Subsection (1) excepts the case where a poll is demanded under section 109. A valid poll displaces the show-of-hands result.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming proof of the number or proportion of votes is required on a show of hands.
misconceptions.correction: Subsection (2) makes the declaration and minute entry conclusive evidence of the fact of passing; the statute does not require such numerical proof for a show of hands.

misconceptions.trap: Confusing show-of-hands voting with electronic voting under section 108 or with poll procedure under section 109.
misconceptions.correction: Section 107 is the default method only when neither a poll under section 109 nor electronic voting applies. Those regimes are separate.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What does section 107 regulate?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Section 107(1) provides that at a general meeting a resolution is decided on a show of hands unless a poll is demanded under section 109 or voting is carried out electronically. Section 107(2) makes the chairman's declaration and the minute-book entry conclusive evidence of the fact of passing of the resolution on a show of hands.
